title: Winter and Cellar
premise: Folklorist Tamsin Okonkwo arrives in the snowbound village of Cellar Hollow to record songs the locals refuse to sing twice, keeping meticulous notes as a private act of devotion to a world that has never made room for him. When an excavation crew unearths a door sealed from the inside beneath the old manor, Tamsin realizes the village's silences are maintenance: something was invited in generations ago and fed ever since. As the longest night approaches, he must survive until sunrise with the truth—that his own arrival was foretold in the songs—while the last resident of the manor, dying and eager to sign the property over, tries to make him the next keeper. Tamsin ends the night by refusing both roles, singing the forbidden songs back to the thing below until dawn breaks it apart, then burning his field notes so the village can finally forget on purpose.
about_author: Vesper Blackwood is the pen name of a former archivist who spent six years cataloguing oral histories in remote coastal and mountain communities before turning to fiction. They write horror about people who listen too carefully.

chapters.title: The Songs They Won't Sing Twice
chapters.summary: Tamsin Okonkwo's POV. He arrives in Cellar Hollow by the last bus before the roads close, renting a room above the post office. The landlady sings him half a lullaby and stops mid-verse, going pale. Emotional beat: wary fascination—the outsider documenting a community that watches him document it.

chapters.title: Field Notes as Prayer
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Over three days he collects fragments: a harvest rhyme missing its final line, a wedding song no one will finish. Each gap matches the others, like verses removed from one longer work. The vicar warns him gently to record weather instead. Emotional beat: growing obsession; documentation becomes devotion.

chapters.title: What the Excavation Turns Up
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, shifting to crew foreman Denny Hale at the end. Crews digging the manor's new foundation strike a stone door, its iron ring fused, sealed from the inside with mortar poured from within. That night every dog in the village faces the manor and howls once, together. Emotional beat: dread arriving on schedule.

chapters.title: The Last Resident
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. He meets Edith Marlowe, ninety-one, the manor's final owner, who is signing papers to sell. She recognizes his surname from the songs and says, 'You're early.' She shows him a ledger of names—one per generation, each marked 'invited.' Emotional beat: the chill of being expected.

chapters.title: Invited In
chapters.summary: Edith's POV, 1958 flashback. Young Edith watched her father perform the Rite of Continuance, singing the completed song down through the door to keep what's below asleep—and learned the rite requires a stranger's voice every fifty years. Emotional beat: love against duty; her father's tenderness and cowardice entwined.

chapters.title: The Village Closes Its Mouth
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The village turns on him: his recordings vanish, the bus won't come back until spring, and someone nails a sprig of rowan over his door—an invitation marker. Denny confesses the crew found handprints on the inside of the sealed door. Emotional beat: isolation sharpening into terror; belonging offered at a price.

chapters.title: Solstice Eve
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Edith, failing fast, begs him to take the ledger and sing the rite at midnight—become the keeper, be safe, be needed. He refuses: he won't buy belonging with someone else's freedom. She signs the papers naming him anyway and dies smiling. Emotional beat: the refusal that dooms and redeems him.

chapters.title: The Longest Night
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The door unseals itself at midnight. Cold climbs the stairs like a tide; the villagers' windows go dark one by one as the thing below calls each name in the ledger—including his. He barricades in Edith's parlor with the recordings playing back her father's rite. Emotional beat: endurance as resistance.

chapters.title: Sung Back
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, climax. Realizing the rite feeds the thing obedience, he does the opposite: he sings the forbidden songs complete, loudly, wrong on purpose, giving it nothing to hold. The village wakes and, hearing their stolen verses finished by an outsider, joins in through the walls. The thing below, starved of fear, unravels toward dawn. Emotional beat: defiant joy; the price of survival refused.

chapters.title: Sunrise Papers
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, epilogue. At dawn the door stands open on empty earth. He burns the ledger and his field notes in the yard while the villagers watch—not erasure this time, but consent. He stays through spring, teaching the children the whole songs. Emotional beat: quiet belonging, finally chosen rather than assigned.
